name: NR (nicotinamide riboside)
summary: A form of vitamin B3 that raises NAD+, a molecule cells use for energy, taken in hopes of healthier aging; trials show few clear health effects.
what_it_is: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a form of vitamin B3 that the body can convert into NAD+, a molecule involved in energy metabolism whose levels decline with age and in many diseases. Taken by mouth, it reliably raises NAD+ in the blood, but there is no sign that it raises NAD+ in muscle; rises in its breakdown products there suggest much of the excess is simply cleared. Some trials have tested it combined with another compound, pterostilbene.

evidence.why: About 25 mostly small human trials show NR raises blood NAD+ and appears safe in the short term, but a 2023 critical review found few clinically relevant effects.

status_us.label: Dietary supplement; GRAS notice for some foods
status_us.note: Used as a dietary supplement. In 2016 FDA had no questions about a company's conclusion that NR is generally recognized as safe (GRAS) as a vitamin B3 source in certain drinks, bars and other foods, though FDA made no GRAS determination of its own.

benefits.claim: Reliably raises NAD+ and related molecules in whole blood in human trials; there is no sign it raises NAD+ in muscle
Modest drops in some blood markers of inflammation, the most consistent effect across trials

No meaningful improvement in insulin sensitivity in several placebo-controlled trials, including detailed clamp studies, and generally no gains in muscle function, exercise performance or body composition
Raised NAD levels in the brain in a placebo-controlled trial of 30 people with newly diagnosed Parkinson's disease; reported symptom gains came only from an after-the-fact subgroup analysis

risks.risk: Blood fats: total and LDL cholesterol rose more than with placebo in a trial of 120 older adults taking NR combined with pterostilbene (clinical relevance uncertain), and triglycerides rose with NR in a placebo-controlled trial of men with obesity
Small drops in potassium, hemoglobin and platelets in an uncontrolled study of 8 volunteers, not seen versus placebo in a heart-failure trial; reviewers judged them not clinically relevant
Long-term safety is unknown: the longest trials of NR alone lasted about 4 to 5 months

avoid_if: High cholesterol or triglycerides (clinician first, especially for products combined with pterostilbene)
interactions: Pterostilbene: the NR-plus-pterostilbene combination raised LDL cholesterol versus placebo in one trial

labs.why: No routine tests are needed and none are evidence-based; trials found kidney markers unchanged, though blood fats rose in some trials, which may matter for people with high cholesterol.

studies.title: What is really known about the effects of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans
studies.people: 25 published human trials of oral NR
studies.finding: NR reliably raised blood NAD+ and appeared safe, but showed few clinically relevant effects; the most consistent was a modest drop in inflammatory markers, and the authors warn that the literature tends to exaggerate effects.

studies.title: Dietary Supplementation With NAD+-Boosting Compounds in Humans: Current Knowledge and Future Directions
studies.people: Human trials of NR, NR with pterostilbene, and NMN
studies.finding: These supplements appear safe and can raise NAD+ in several tissues, but evidence that they improve physiological function is unclear, and small trials limit conclusions.

ask_your_clinician: Given how few clinical effects trials have shown, is there a measurable reason to expect NR to help me?
Should I avoid NR products combined with pterostilbene because of my cholesterol?
Do any of my conditions or medicines make an NAD+ booster a bad idea?

notes_for_editor: The main source is a critical 2023 narrative review (Science Advances) that does not pool data; trial sizes and funding were not tabulated in what was read. The GRAS letter covers use in foods, not supplements, and FDA said it did not consider whether drug-related rules (section 301(ll)) apply; FDA's new dietary ingredient records for NR were not opened. No source opened addressed pregnancy, liver injury or drug interactions for NR alone; LiverTox was not checked. Brand names in the catalog aliases are not used.
